group.title: Abstract ideas
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The state of having more than one possible meaning.
examples: The {ambiguity} of the law caused problems.
wrong: Ambiguity is the quality of being perfectly clear and exact.

words.meaning: The freedom to make your own decisions.
examples: The new manager gave the team more {autonomy}.
wrong: Autonomy is the lack of any freedom to choose.

words.meaning: The quality of being logical and well connected.
examples: The essay lacks {coherence}.
wrong: Coherence is the absence of any logic between ideas.

words.meaning: The state of having many connected parts.
examples: I did not understand the {complexity} of the problem.
wrong: Complexity means that something is very simple with only one part.

words.meaning: Something that limits what you can do.
examples: Lack of time was a major {constraint}.
wrong: A constraint is something that gives you unlimited freedom.

words.meaning: A connection between two things that change together.
examples: There is a {correlation} between sleep and test scores.
wrong: A correlation means two things have nothing to do with each other.

words.meaning: A difficult choice between two options.
examples: She faced a {dilemma}: stay or leave.
wrong: A dilemma is an easy choice with only one good answer.

words.meaning: A difference between things that should be the same.
examples: There was a {discrepancy} in the accounts.
wrong: A discrepancy is a perfect match with no difference.

words.meaning: A clear difference between two things.
examples: There is a clear {distinction} between a fact and an opinion.
wrong: A distinction is a similarity so complete that no difference exists.

words.meaning: A state of balance.
examples: The market returned to {equilibrium}.
wrong: Equilibrium is a state of wild and uneven change.

words.meaning: A system in which people or things are ranked above others.
examples: The army has a strict {hierarchy}.
wrong: A hierarchy is a system in which everyone has exactly the same rank.

words.meaning: Understanding something only after it has happened.
examples: With {hindsight}, we should have left earlier.
wrong: Hindsight is the ability to see exactly what will happen in the future.

words.meaning: A possible effect or meaning that is not stated directly.
examples: The {implication} of his words was clear.
wrong: An implication is something that is stated directly and loudly.

words.meaning: A lack of agreement between things.
examples: I found an {inconsistency} in her story.
wrong: An inconsistency is a complete match between all the parts.

words.meaning: The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles.
examples: He is a man of {integrity}.
wrong: Integrity is the habit of lying whenever it is useful.

words.meaning: Something handed down from the past.
examples: The artist left a lasting {legacy}.
wrong: A legacy is something that disappears at once and leaves nothing.

words.meaning: The great size or importance of something.
examples: We did not understand the {magnitude} of the problem.
wrong: Magnitude is the tiny size of something unimportant.

words.meaning: The force that keeps something moving or growing.
examples: The campaign gained {momentum} quickly.
wrong: Momentum is the loss of all movement and energy.

words.meaning: A small difference in meaning or tone.
examples: A good translator captures every {nuance}.
wrong: A nuance is a big and obvious difference.

words.meaning: A statement or situation that seems impossible but may be true.
examples: It is a {paradox} that more choice can make us unhappy.
wrong: A paradox is a plain fact that nobody finds strange.

words.meaning: An earlier case used as a guide for later ones.
examples: The judge’s decision set a {precedent}.
wrong: A precedent is a case that happens after all the others and is never used.

words.meaning: An idea on which an argument is based.
examples: The argument rests on a false {premise}.
wrong: A premise is the final result at the end of an argument.

words.meaning: Nearness in space or time.
examples: The hotel’s {proximity} to the station is a benefit.
wrong: Proximity means a great distance between two places.

words.meaning: The reasons behind a decision.
examples: She explained the {rationale} for the change.
wrong: A rationale is a decision made with no reasons at all.

words.meaning: The range of things that something covers.
examples: The {scope} of the project is very wide.
wrong: The scope of a project is the exact money it costs.

words.meaning: A general feeling or opinion.
examples: Public {sentiment} is against the plan.
wrong: Sentiment is a hard fact that can be measured with a ruler.

words.meaning: Money given by a government to help an industry.
examples: Farmers receive a {subsidy} from the state.
wrong: A subsidy is a tax that people pay to a shop.

words.meaning: The combining of separate ideas into a whole.
examples: The book is a {synthesis} of many theories.
wrong: A synthesis is the splitting of an idea into separate pieces with no joining.

words.meaning: The level at which something starts to happen.
examples: Sales passed the {threshold} of one million.
wrong: A threshold is the highest point that nobody can reach.

words.meaning: Willingness to accept different opinions or behavior.
examples: A good society shows {tolerance} toward others.
wrong: Tolerance is a strong dislike of anyone who is different.

words.meaning: The path that something follows over time.
examples: The company’s {trajectory} is upward.
wrong: A trajectory is a place where nothing moves at all.

words.meaning: Openness, so that others can see what is happening.
examples: Voters want more {transparency} from the government.
wrong: Transparency means that decisions are kept secret from everyone.

words.meaning: The state of being easily harmed.
examples: The report shows the {vulnerability} of old systems.
wrong: Vulnerability is the state of being completely safe.

words.meaning: An unfair opinion about a person or a group.
examples: She fought against {prejudice} in her town.
wrong: Prejudice is a fair opinion that comes after careful study.

words.meaning: The ability to recover quickly from difficulties.
examples: The community showed great {resilience} after the flood.
wrong: Resilience is the habit of giving up at the first problem.

words.meaning: Moral principles about right and wrong.
examples: Doctors follow strict medical {ethics}.
wrong: Ethics is a set of rules for cooking.

words.meaning: The duty to explain and take responsibility for your actions.
examples: Voters demand {accountability} from their leaders.
wrong: Accountability is the freedom to avoid any blame.

words.meaning: Something that is different from what is normal.
examples: The result was an {anomaly} in the data.
wrong: An anomaly is a normal result that fits the pattern.

words.meaning: A mark of shame that society attaches to something.
examples: There is still a {stigma} about mental illness.
wrong: A stigma is a mark of great honor that everyone praises.

words.meaning: The power to influence a situation.
examples: The union has little {leverage} in the talks.
wrong: Leverage is the lack of any power over others.

words.meaning: A typical model or pattern of how something works.
examples: The discovery changed the scientific {paradigm}.
wrong: A paradigm is a very small mistake in a sentence.
